data.name: A Week of Circus Terror
data.detailed_description:
DESCRIPTION

As well as an unexplained suicide of his owner in the 50s, the house has woken up after 40 years and the visitor Gerald is determined to solve the whole secret about the disappearance of his son and in the meanwhile he is also trying to find out something about the owner's horrible history and history of the house.
As the night is about to begin, your task is to survive the night and find some informations about your lost son. When the last sun rays disappear, the night will start and the terror will begin.

Genre: Horror, Indie.
Made by Clickteam Fusion 2.5.
This game contains clowns! Also scary sounds, environment or animations (sick jumpscares).


BONUSES

Achievements: There are fifteen game (not Steam) achievements and each of them has different ways to complete it.
Score: If you successfully resist against the one antagonist, you get one score. If you don't resist against the antagonist, you won't get any score for that moment.
Every survived night confirms the score for that night. If you fail, the score for that night resets and you have to play it again.
Also score is seperated to nights from 1 to 10 and to nights from 11 to 13 and this function has nothing to do with the story.


HOW TO PLAY

Use your mouse (left click) for moving to the other rooms of the house. Sometimes (in a situation) you can click on the objects or „something weird“.
For the flashlight press „F“, for turning on the light bulb press and hold „Ctrl“, for using the map press „M“ and for leave the game or go to menu press „Esc“ .
(There is no pause menu).


RESOLUTION, COMPUTER SETTINGS

Better computer means faster moving, faster time passing in nights and transition between rooms or frames.
When you start this game, the game automatically sets to full Screen.
If you want to change the resolution of the game, press ALT + ENTER.

Also this is my first official made game.
I didn't have experiences with creating the game, or even animations.
But, enjoy!

data.short_description: A hand-drawn, point & click indie horror game about the haunted house and his owner. During the day, you have to search for some informations, but when the night comes, you have to understand, why are the possessed toys trying to kill you. You have to find a way to go through them and save your life!

reviews.review:
A Week of Circus Terror is an independently produced horror experience that mixes point-and-click investigation with survival-oriented nighttime encounters. Developed and published by Richard Haraším, it has the unmistakable qualities of a personal solo project, favoring unusual ideas and handcrafted presentation over technical sophistication. The premise revolves around an old house with a disturbing history, and the game gradually turns that location into both a mystery to investigate and a dangerous environment to survive.

The story follows Gerald as he searches for his missing son, eventually becoming involved with a house connected to a suicide that occurred decades earlier. The building's past provides the foundation for the supernatural events that follow, and discovering what happened becomes an important part of Gerald's investigation. It is a straightforward setup, but it gives the player a meaningful reason to examine rooms, interact with suspicious objects, and pay attention to clues rather than treating the house as nothing more than a backdrop for scares.

One of the game's defining ideas is its division between daytime investigation and nighttime survival. During the safer periods, the emphasis is placed on exploration and gathering information. Once darkness arrives, the atmosphere changes considerably as possessed toys and other threatening entities become active. Surviving these encounters requires awareness of what is happening around the house and an understanding of how individual threats behave. This creates a repeating rhythm in which exploration builds tension before the night provides the more immediate danger.

Navigation and interaction are intentionally uncomplicated. Much of the experience uses mouse-driven movement between locations, while environmental objects can be selected when interaction is possible. The player also has access to practical tools such as a flashlight, room lighting, and a map. Consequently, this is not a conventional free-roaming first-person horror game. Its design is closer to a collection of interconnected scenes where observation, interaction, and responding correctly to threats are more important than physically navigating a detailed 3D environment.

Nighttime encounters are supported by a scoring system. Successfully dealing with an antagonist can award points, while mistakes cost the opportunity to gain them. Surviving an entire night secures the score accumulated during that period, whereas failure forces the player to repeat the night and lose the progress made toward that particular score. The scoring system is separate from the main story, so players interested primarily in discovering the mystery are not required to obsess over perfect performance. For those who enjoy mastering enemy behavior, however, it provides additional replay value.

There are also fifteen built-in achievements with different requirements. These are internal game accomplishments rather than Steam achievements, but they offer another layer of optional objectives for completion-focused players. Together with the scoring mechanics, they encourage experimentation beyond simply reaching the end of the narrative. This is useful because the core gameplay itself is relatively simple, and additional challenges help provide some incentive to replay sections after learning how their threats operate.

The atmosphere relies heavily on sinister toys, clown imagery, unsettling sounds, strange animations, dark rooms, and sudden jump scares. The horror is generally direct rather than restrained. Players who dislike frequent shock-based scares may find some sequences predictable, but the handmade visual approach gives the game a peculiar identity. The rough artwork can occasionally make creatures look unintentionally awkward, yet that same awkwardness sometimes works surprisingly well because the characters and objects feel abnormal in ways that cleaner graphics might not reproduce.

Technical and presentation limitations are considerably more noticeable. This was created as an early game-development effort, and the lack of extensive production experience can be seen in the animation, interface, visual consistency, and general refinement. Hardware performance can also influence certain aspects of gameplay speed, potentially affecting movement and the pacing of nighttime sequences. That is an unusual technical characteristic and means the experience may not behave identically across every computer. The absence of some modern interface conveniences further reinforces its experimental, low-budget character.

Steam Deck compatibility is not officially verified, so it should not be considered a guaranteed Deck-ready experience. Its relatively straightforward mouse and keyboard control scheme may be adaptable through Steam Input, particularly by assigning trackpad or analog controls to mouse functions and mapping keyboard commands manually. However, because the game was designed around desktop input and has unusual performance-dependent behavior, players should expect that configuration or experimentation may be necessary. Until an official Steam Deck rating or reliable native handheld optimization is provided, its compatibility is best regarded as unverified rather than fully supported.

As a complete package, A Week of Circus Terror succeeds more through personality and ambition than polish. The alternating investigation and survival structure is an interesting foundation, while the scoring mechanics, optional achievements, haunted-house mystery, and assortment of supernatural enemies give the game more substance than its simple appearance initially suggests. Its weaknesses come from limited production values, basic interaction, uneven technical behavior, rough animation, and a reliance on familiar horror devices.

Players interested in polished modern horror will probably find the experience too primitive, but enthusiasts of obscure indie projects may appreciate its handcrafted quality and unconventional design. There is something compelling about seeing a small horror concept attempt to combine mystery, survival, scoring, and point-and-click mechanics within a single haunted setting. It is imperfect and clearly experimental, yet it possesses enough individuality to make it an interesting curiosity for players who enjoy exploring the rougher edges of independent horror development.

Rating: 5/10
